title: Pair & Mob Programming
summary: Real-time collaborative coding — driver/navigator, strong-style, ping-pong, and whole-team mobbing — as an alternative to async review, with an honest account of what it costs and when it's worth it.

slides.markdown:
Async code review moves feedback to *after* the code is written. Pairing moves it to *while* it's being written — which changes what feedback is even possible, because you can redirect a design before it exists rather than asking for a rewrite afterwards.

The honest framing: pairing costs roughly two engineers' time for one engineer's output, and buys review, knowledge transfer, and design correction in the same pass. Sometimes that's a bargain and sometimes it's waste, and knowing which is the actual skill.

This topic covers the mechanics that make pairing work — driver/navigator, strong-style, ping-pong, mobbing — plus remote etiquette, where pairing pays off most, and the failure modes teams hit when they adopt it uncritically.

slides.subTitle: Two roles, one keyboard
slides.markdown:
The **driver** has the keyboard and handles the tactical layer: syntax, the current function, making the test pass. The **navigator** doesn't type and works one level up — is this the right approach, what breaks at the boundary, is there an existing helper for this, what's the next test.

The reason the roles are named at all is that without them both people default to driving, which produces backseat typing ("no, semicolon, no — *there*") and neither person doing the thinking.

What separates real pairing from two people watching one screen:

- **Swap the keyboard every 15–30 minutes**, on a timer. Whoever drives longest disengages the other one.
- **The navigator's job is questions, not corrections.** "What happens if that list is empty?" beats "you need a null check." The first keeps the driver thinking; the second turns them into a typist.
- **Let small mistakes go.** Interrupting a typo destroys the driver's flow for a thing the compiler would have caught in four seconds.

The tight loop is the whole value: a wrong turn is caught in seconds, not in tomorrow's review comments after it's been built on.

slides.subTitle: Two protocols worth knowing by name
slides.markdown:
Generic "take turns" pairing drifts. Two named protocols fix specific failures.

**Strong-style pairing** (Llewellyn Falco): *"for an idea to go from your head into the computer, it must go through someone else's hands."* The person with the idea navigates; the other person types. It sounds backwards and it's the single best tool for pairing across an experience gap — the senior cannot silently take over, because they're not allowed to touch the keyboard, and the junior's hands are on every line so they can't spectate.

**Ping-pong pairing** binds the swap to TDD:

1. A writes a failing test.
2. B makes it pass, then writes the next failing test.
3. A makes it pass, writes the next. Repeat.

The swap point is structural rather than a timer someone ignores, and each person alternates between specifying behavior and implementing it — so neither settles into one role.

Use strong-style when the experience gap is wide or you're teaching a codebase. Use ping-pong when both are peers on well-understood work and you want an even split without policing it.

slides.subTitle: The whole team, one problem
slides.markdown:
**Mobbing** (or ensemble programming) is the whole team — typically three to six people — on one problem at one keyboard, with the driver rotating on a strict timer, often 4–7 minutes via a tool like `mobster` or `mob.sh`.

The economics look absurd and occasionally aren't. Five engineers on one task is five times the cost per hour, but you also get: zero handoffs, zero code review queue, no context reconstruction, and every decision made with everyone present, so nobody has to be re-convinced later.

Where it genuinely earns its cost:

- **A gnarly production bug** nobody has cracked alone — five perspectives converge faster than five sequential attempts.
- **Kicking off an unfamiliar subsystem**, where the design decisions in the first two days shape the next six months.
- **Onboarding several people at once** into a codebase.
- **A cross-cutting change** touching four services owned by four people.

Where it's waste: routine CRUD work, anything one person already knows how to do, and anything where four of the five participants are silently waiting for their turn to type. If people are checking Slack, the mob has become a meeting.

Most teams that use mobbing use it in bursts — half a day on the hard thing, not as the default mode.

slides.subTitle: Different feedback, different cost
slides.markdown:
These aren't the same activity done at different times — the feedback they can produce is genuinely different:

| | Pairing | Async review |
|---|---|---|
| **When feedback lands** | as the code is written | after it's finished |
| **Cost** | 2 engineers × the full duration | ~30–60 min of one reviewer |
| **Catches best** | wrong approach, wrong abstraction, wrong problem | defects, edge cases, missing tests |
| **Cost of a redirect** | seconds — nothing is built yet | a rewrite, and the author is invested |
| **Record** | none unless you write one | permanent, searchable, linked to the diff |
| **Reviewer's context** | full — they watched it happen | reconstructed from the diff |
| **Scheduling** | needs synchronized calendars | none |

The decisive asymmetry is the redirect cost. Catching "this whole approach is wrong" at minute five costs nothing; catching it in review costs a day and lands on someone who has already built a case for their design.

But async review leaves a **written record** — why a change was made, what was considered, who signed off — which pairing loses entirely unless someone deliberately writes it down. That's not a small loss when you're debugging this code in eighteen months.

slides.subTitle: Tools and etiquette
slides.markdown:
Remote pairing is not screen-sharing at someone. The distinction that matters is whether the non-driver can **act** — move the cursor, jump to a definition, edit — or only watch.

- **VS Code Live Share / JetBrains Code With Me** — each person keeps their own keybindings and theme, and can navigate independently. Best for wide-gap pairing where the junior needs to explore without stealing the keyboard.
- **Tuple, Pop** — low-latency screen share with remote control. Feels like one machine.
- **`tmux` over SSH** — free, keyboard-latency-free, and terminal-only:

```bash
# host
tmux new -s pair
tmux server-access -a teammate   # tmux 3.3+, shared socket
# guest, after ssh to the same box
tmux attach -t pair
```

The etiquette that decides whether it works:

- **Camera on for the first minutes at least.** Text and voice alone lose the confusion signal, which is the thing the navigator most needs to see.
- **Narrate before you type.** "I'm going to extract this into a helper" — otherwise the other person is reverse-engineering your intent from a cursor.
- **Say when you need silence.** "Give me two minutes on this loop" is a normal and useful sentence.
- **Schedule an end time.** Remote pairing without one runs long and burns people out faster than in-person.

slides.subTitle: The knowledge docs can't carry
slides.markdown:
Documentation transfers facts. Pairing transfers the things nobody wrote down and probably couldn't:

- **Which parts of the codebase are dangerous.** "Don't touch that module without talking to Priya" is never in a README.
- **How to debug here** — which log stream, which dashboard, which staging box, which incantation actually reproduces the bug.
- **The unwritten conventions.** Why this service uses a repository pattern and that one deliberately doesn't.
- **Search strategy.** Watching someone navigate an unfamiliar 400k-line repo is a skill transfer that no onboarding doc attempts.

A new hire pairing on real tickets for their first two weeks typically reaches independent productivity noticeably faster than one working alone through a doc-and-starter-ticket path — and the difference is mostly that they stop losing hours to questions they didn't know to ask.

**Use strong-style here specifically.** The onboarding failure mode is the senior taking the keyboard "just to get past this bit" and the new hire spending two weeks watching. Hands on the keyboard, ideas from the navigator — the protocol enforces what good intentions don't.

One caution: pair a new hire with a *rotation* of teammates, not one buddy. Otherwise they inherit exactly one person's mental model, blind spots included.

slides.subTitle: And when it's two people doing one job
slides.markdown:
Pairing costs about 2x the engineer-hours for maybe 1.1–1.2x the throughput on routine work. That's a bad trade on routine work and a clear win where the alternative is expensive.

**High value:**

- **A bug that has beaten one person for a day.** The second pair of eyes breaks fixation, which is the actual failure mode — you stop being able to see the assumption you made an hour ago.
- **Design-in-progress**, where the shape isn't decided. Redirecting a design costs seconds during pairing and a day in review.
- **High-blast-radius code** — payments, auth, migrations. Two people who both understand it beats one who does plus one who approved a diff.
- **Onboarding and deliberate knowledge spreading** off a bus-factor-of-one subsystem.

**Overkill:**

- Routine CRUD, boilerplate, or a well-understood refactor.
- Anything where one person already knows the answer and the other is watching them type it.
- Exploratory spikes — reading docs and trying things is faster alone, then pair on what you learned.

The test I'd apply: **would this change get a genuinely careful async review anyway?** If yes, pairing is probably redundant. If it's the kind of change that gets an LGTM in four minutes and shouldn't, pair on it.

slides.subTitle: The cost nobody budgets for
slides.markdown:
Six hours of pairing is far more draining than six hours of solo work, and teams that adopt pairing enthusiastically without accounting for that burn people out in about a month, then conclude pairing doesn't work.

The reason is that pairing removes every micro-break — no drifting for thirty seconds, no checking a thing, no thinking with your eyes closed. Sustained social and cognitive load with no gaps, plus the constant low-level performance of thinking out loud.

What makes it sustainable:

- **Cap it around 4–5 hours a day**, not 8. The remaining time is for solo work, email, and thinking.
- **Real breaks on a timer** — 10 minutes every hour, or a Pomodoro cadence. Skipping breaks because you're in flow is the main way this goes wrong.
- **Nobody pairs 100% of the time.** Some work genuinely is better alone, and some people need substantially more solo time to do their best thinking. That's a legitimate working style, not low engagement.
- **Let people opt out of a session** without it being a statement.

If a team's pairing enthusiasm collapses after a few weeks, exhaustion is the usual explanation — not a verdict on the practice.

slides.subTitle: Where the value leaks
slides.markdown:
Left to self-organize, pairs form by comfort: the two seniors who think alike pair on the interesting problem, and the juniors get async review comments.

This inverts the value. Senior–senior pairing on well-understood work is the *lowest*-return pairing available — both already know the codebase, so the knowledge transfer is near zero and you've spent 2x for a marginal quality gain. Meanwhile the pairing that would move the team most is exactly the one nobody scheduled.

Rough value ranking:

- **Senior + junior** — highest return. Knowledge flows, and the junior's questions routinely surface assumptions the senior stopped seeing.
- **Mid + mid** — good. Genuinely different approaches, neither defers.
- **Senior + senior** — worth it only on genuinely hard or high-stakes problems.

The fix is to stop leaving it to self-organization: rotate pairs on a schedule, and pair across the experience gap on the *interesting* work, not just the maintenance ticket. Use strong-style there so the senior can't quietly take over.

The cultural version of this failure is worse — juniors get feedback only as review comments, which is the lowest-bandwidth channel available, and then people wonder why they're growing slowly.

Partly. Pairing does most of what review does — a second engineer evaluated every line, in more depth than a diff reader ever will — so requiring a full second review of paired code is usually theater.

What it does **not** replace:

- **The written record.** A PR captures why a change was made and what was rejected. A pairing session captures none of that unless someone writes it up, and "we discussed it" is a poor answer eighteen months later.
- **Fresh eyes.** Two people who designed something together share the same blind spot by construction. A reader with no investment sees things neither of you can.
- **Compliance.** SOX, PCI-DSS and similar regimes often require a documented approval by someone other than the author, and "we paired" doesn't satisfy an auditor without a trail.

The practical middle ground most teams land on: paired work still opens a PR, tagged as paired with `Co-authored-by:` trailers in the commit, and gets a **lighter** review — a fresh-eyes pass for defects rather than a full design review. That keeps the audit trail and the outside perspective while not paying twice for the same scrutiny.

And add the design rationale to the PR description. That's the piece pairing genuinely loses.

The mature position isn't "we pair" or "we don't" — it's picking the collaboration mode per piece of work:

- **Solo plus async review** — the default. Routine work, well-understood changes.
- **Pairing** — hard bugs, design-in-progress, high-blast-radius code, onboarding, deliberate bus-factor reduction.
- **Mobbing** — cross-cutting changes, the bug nobody has cracked, kicking off an unfamiliar subsystem.

A team that pairs on everything is overspending; a team that never pairs is paying for it in review latency, concentrated knowledge, and juniors who only ever get feedback as comments on a diff.

What makes this work in practice is the protocols, not the intention — strong-style across an experience gap, ping-pong between peers, timed driver rotation in a mob, and a cap on how many hours a day anyone pairs.
